title: Is Social Media Addiction a Clinical Reality?
author: Meshi, Dar
summary: A California court awarded six million dollars for social media 'addiction' while the psychiatric community has not yet agreed this constitutes a clinical disorder. The gap between legal, rhetorical, and medical categories matters profoundly. When legal language races ahead of medical consensus, and therapeutic language outpaces both, the word 'disorder' shifts from a tool of care to an instrument of persuasion. Theologically, calling every compulsion a disease outsources moral agency to machinery, relieving users of harder questions about their attention and intentionality.
points: Legal judgments now recognize social media addiction harms while clinicians lack consensus on whether it constitutes a diagnosable disorder.
When legal categories race ahead of medical ones, disorder language becomes persuasive rhetoric rather than precise diagnostic tool.
Calling every compulsion a disease outsources moral agency to technology, avoiding harder questions about human choice and attention.
The diagnostic category matters because it shapes whether people understand themselves as afflicted or accountable for their choices.
Medicine must maintain distinction between descriptive diagnosis and moral categories, lest treatment language become mere excuse-making.
quotes: A California jury recently awarded six million dollars for the harm caused by 'addictive' social media platforms, even as working psychiatrists caution that the clinical community has not yet agreed that the social media use constitutes an addiction.

The gap matters. When the legal category races ahead of the medical one, and the rhetorical category races ahead of both, the word 'disorder' begins to function less as a tool of care and more as an instrument of persuasion.
To call every compulsion a disease is to quietly outsource moral agency to the machinery, which relieves the user of the harder question of what he is doing with his attention and why.
The deeper problem is theological in its implications.” Archived from Neuroscience News on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
